title: Air Pressure by Elevation Calculator
description: Estimate standard-atmosphere air pressure at any elevation with the Air Pressure by Elevation Calculator — kPa, hPa and percent of sea level. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, at Denver's 1,609 metres the standard atmosphere gives 83.4 kPa — about 82% of sea-level pressure — which is why a sealed snack bag puffs up on the drive into the mountains.
quick_answer: The Air Pressure by Elevation Calculator applies the international standard atmosphere to estimate air pressure at a given elevation. Enter the height and read the pressure in kilopascals, hectopascals and percent of sea level — a weather-free reference value that pilots, hikers and engineers start from.

At 3,000 m the air holds about 69% of sea-level pressure. Breathing, boiling and engine performance all follow that number — the
Air density scales with pressure; a fan sized at sea level moves thinner air in Albuquerque. Standard pressure is the first correction.
The exponential decay of the atmosphere is this curve — half the air below ~5,500 m, three quarters below ~11,000 m, computed from the same formula.
At about 5,500 m the standard pressure is 50.5 kPa — half of sea level. Half of the entire atmosphere's mass sits below that height, which Everest base-camp trekkers feel in every step.

At 8,849 m the standard atmosphere gives about 31 kPa — roughly one third of sea-level pressure (real summit measurements average a little higher, around 34 kPa, because Everest's latitude bulges the atmosphere). Model versus mountain, honestly labelled.

popular_table.title: Standard pressure by elevation
popular_table.intro: From the standard-atmosphere formula this calculator uses (troposphere model).
popular_table.note: The standard atmosphere assumes a fixed temperature profile (15°C at sea level, cooling 6.5°C per km). Real pressure at your height today also rides on weather systems — see the FAQs.

faq: The international standard atmosphere's troposphere formula: pressure = 101,325 × (1 − 2.25577×10⁻⁵ × height in metres)^5.25588 pascals. It models an average atmosphere, not today's sky.
How fast does pressure drop near the ground?
About 1 hPa per 8.3 metres (roughly 1 inHg per 300 m) in the lowest layers — the rule altimeter pilots feel on climb-out — slowing as the air thins.
My barometer disagrees with the table.
It should, a little: weather moves real surface pressure ±3% routinely. Barometers report now; this calculator reports standard. The gap between them is literally the weather.
Pressure altitude is the height the standard atmosphere assigns to a measured pressure. Aviation flies by it so that all aircraft share one ruler; this calculator's curve is that ruler.
In reality yes — warm air is thicker, so pressure falls more slowly with height on hot days. The standard model fixes a reference temperature profile so values stay comparable.
Millimetres of mercury and inHg follow fixed factors (101.325 kPa = 760 mmHg = 29.92 inHg) — the standard sea-level row of the table is the conversion key.
